35851.sectionTitle: Recommendations w hen Using Correlation Coefficients
35851.content:
24.6 Recommendations w hen Using Correlation Coefficients
When investigating relationships between variables with statistics such as those described in
this chapter, the following points should be kept in mind:
n A large value of a correlation coefficient is not, by itself, meaningful; the significance
of the coefficient is a function of sample size.
n The presence of a significant correlation between two variables does not necessarily
imply a cause-and-effect relationship.
n The value of any correlation coefficient is meaningless if the assumptions on which it
is based are not satisfied by the data being analyzed.

In the previous chapter, we developed a measure for the degree of correspondence or
relationship between two variables. These types of statistics provide information about the
degree and, sometimes, the direction of the relationship. However, we can go beyond cor-
relation analysis to predict, with known accuracy, the value of one of the variables when the
value of the other is known. This prediction process is called regression.
The word “regression” comes from the first study that used the concept, which was published
by Sir Francis Galton in 1885.

In the study, Galton examined the relationship between
heights of parents and their children and found that the heights of children of unusually tall
or short parents tended toward the average height of the population; that is, their heights
regressed toward the average height. Regression has come to mean the prediction of the
value of a variable from the values of one or more other variables.
Consider the simplest case, in which we have collected value pairs for two variables, X and Y,
and we wish to predict the value of Y that might correspond to a given value of X.

Regression analyses serve three purposes in statistical research: description, statistical con-
trol, and prediction. In some situations, previously collected data is examined to discover the
relationship between some dependent quantity and one or more independent variables. In
these cases, description is the goal.
In a study of the relationship between two variables, the researcher can use regression analy-
sis to statistically control the influence of some other quantity. For example, in a study of two
marketing strategies, surveys might be administered after each quarter. Regression equa-
tions can be found to relate the marketing strategy performance ratings to sales personnel,
and these equations can be used to adjust the ratings, inflating those sales personnel with
limited field experience and deflating those sales personnel with years of field experience.
Remaining differences in performance ratings are then due to differences in the two market-
ing strategies.
Finally, a regression equation can be used to predict the value of a variable from the value of
some other quantity, as in predicting sales averages from amount of advertisement funding.

Artificial Neural Networks and Multiple Linear Regression Models
A neural network is essentially a way of simulating a human brain’s activity. The brain is
composed of billions of units referred to as neurons. Each neuron is connected to other
neurons and communicates with them through electrochemical signals. These signals
are captured by synapses, or end branches to the neuron’s cell, called dendrites. Neu-
rons sum up the inputs from the synapses, the inputs, and output a signal on a tail, to the
neuron, referred to as an axon. Artificial neurons are simply an electronic simulation of
biological neurons.
Each artificial neuron acts similar to the Kelley-Salisbury algorithm for a multiple linear
regression equation. When input signals are triggered to the artificial neuron, then the
sum of the weighted input values is submitted to the artificial neuron and an output sig-
nal is activated if it is greater than a threshold value.
In order to link many neurons together, one can start with an initial design of neurons
which are organized into layers. These layers feed their output forward to the next layer
until linking to the final output from the neural network. Input is sent to each neuron in
the innermost layer, actually a hidden layer, and then each hidden layer’s neuron output
is sent to every neuron in the next layer. Such a neural network, referred to as a feed
forward network can have any number of hidden layers.
Neural networks have to be trained. As with the Kelley-Salisbury algorithm for multiple
linear regression, one way of training a neural network is with randomly assigned input
weights. Then a series of inputs, representative of the final desired outputs, are fed into
the artificial neural network. For each configuration of inputs one checks the output

36006.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36006.heading: ON DVD
36006.content:
and adjust the weights accordingly until the network successively recognizes the desired
result. The approach overview in this discussion is referred to as supervised learning.
The data fed into the artificial neural network during training is the training set.
It should be noted that the Kelley-Salisbury algorithm for multiple linear regression
employs only one output, whereas even the simplest neural network, a perception, can
have one or more outputs. Each output has a separate bias and set of weights. Actually,
a perception with a linear activation function is a linear regression model and a percep-
tion with a logistic function is a logistic regression model. In fact, to be more explicit, a
perception with a threshold activation function is a linear discriminant function. With
multiple outputs, the threshold perception is a multiple discriminant function.
Another major difference between artificial neural networks and multiple linear regres-
sion is the number of coefficients per input. Regression coefficients are determined
by the method of least squared error, an optimization technique, whereas, neural nets
employ the method of gradient descent, which allows for multiple coefficients per input.

There are other methods used to determine which independent variables should be retained
in a regression model. The most popular of these is stepwise regression, in which a sequence
of regression equations is constructed. At each step, an independent variable is added to or
deleted from the model.
Forward stepwise regression begins by including in the regression equation only the single
independent variable that by itself produces the largest coefficient of determination R
2
as
measured by an F test. In the second step, another predictor is added to the developing
equation, one that with the predictor of the first step produces the largest value of R
2
. This
second step is then iterated, including one new predictor at each repetition until all are
included in the final full model. The predictors entered first are the most important, and we
can gauge the relative importance of predictors by watching R
2
increase at each step of the
development.
The stepwise regression process also allows predictors to be removed from the equation. If
subsequent inclusions have made earlier additions unimportant, this assumes that there is a
single “best” set of predictors and we seek to identify them in the full model.
Stepwise regression can also be extended to forward and backward set selection, in which
the researcher selects sets of predictors to be included and deleted at each step.

36080.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36080.heading: 29.3 Forward, s tepwise, and b ackward s election
36080.sectionTitle: Forward, s tepwise, and b ackward s election
36080.content:
29.3 Forward, s tepwise, and b ackward s election
Most statistical packages use a variety of criteria for determining what subset of variables
will be used as predictors in a regression model. Forward selection, backward elimination,
and stepwise algorithms are commonly employed for the selection process. The selection
criteria are usually based on the significance of the partial F statistic or on the increases of
the multiple coefficient of determination when a variable is to be added to a candidate list of
predictors. The potential predictor variables are added or deleted one at a time or they may
be exchanged for one of the other predictor variables.

36081.title: researchmethodsforinformationsystems
36081.heading: 29.3.1 Forward selection
36081.content:
29.3.1 Forward selection
This is an automated, or software controlled, selection of predictor variables method. The
method starts by completing simple regression analysis utilizing the single “best” predictor,
or the predictor with the largest R
2
value. Next the predictor with the largest partial F value
is chosen and a two-variable multiple linear regression analysis is performed. This process
of adding predictors is continued until all variables have been added, or until the largest
remaining partial F value is too small to consider as statistically significant. One of the prob-
lems with this approach is that it is possible to have several predictors that are nonsignificant
at an early step in this process and then all become significant at a later step in the process.
Note that once a predictor variable is added to the model, then that variable permanently
remains in the model from that step forward.
364 n n n r e S earch Method S F or In F or M at I on Sy S te MS n c Hapter 29
29.3.2 s tepwise selection
In the stepwise selection algorithm any predictor variable having a partial F value not greater
than or equal to a minimal significance level is dropped from the model and placed in the
queue of candidates for forward selection and are, thus, eligible for re-inclusion in the model
at a later stage in the process.
29.3.3 b ackward elimination
A major problem with forward selection and stepwise selection is that a set of variates which
jointly predict the criterion variable, yet individually have little to no prediction on the
criterion variable, will cause trouble. Neither forward nor stepwise selection will discover
the joint prediction for these predictors since both selection methods assume that the vari-
able to be entered at any step is nonsignificant. As a result, any weaker variable cannot be
significant.
Backward elimination starts with all predictor variables in the model, then variables are
removed one at a time based upon providing the smallest partial F value. This procedure ter-
minates when all partial F values are significant at a threshold value for staying in the model.
Note that the backward elimination method will discover a set of variates which jointly pre-
dict the criterion variable yet individually have little or no predictive value for the criterion
variable since their joint prediction value will be evident. Only the backward elimination
algorithm allows for the discovery of such jointly strong predictor sets.
Good material on the selection methods are Stepwise regression from Wikipedia at http://
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stepwise_regression and Simplifying a Multiple Regression Equation
at http://www.jerrydallai.com/LHSP/simplify.htm.
